misconceptions.description: Assuming that a method which saves time is automatically more equitable for all students
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites time saved as proof of fairness without checking how benefits and harms are distributed
misconceptions.feedback: Run the equity check separately: sample a vulnerable subgroup's results and see whether the efficient method distributes harm evenly. Time saved is not an equity claim.

misconceptions.description: Treating identical treatment of all students as equity, ignoring different starting conditions
misconceptions.trigger: learner gives everyone the same tool or task 'to be fair' and ignores resource gaps that produce unequal outcomes
misconceptions.feedback: Distinguish equal from equitable. When starting conditions differ, identical treatment can widen gaps; equity reallocates resources to close them.

misconceptions.description: Believing an AI ranking is unbiased simply because it is data-driven, without inspecting whether its inputs encode existing disadvantage
misconceptions.trigger: learner allocates support strictly by an AI risk ranking without interrogating its inputs
misconceptions.feedback: Interrogate the inputs. Attendance and prior grades can encode jobs, caregiving, or prior inequity. Adjust before letting the ranking drive resources.

misconceptions.description: Treating efficiency as a value that automatically overrides equity rather than one to be balanced against it
misconceptions.trigger: learner rejects a slower but more equitable option solely because a faster one exists
misconceptions.feedback: A defensible balance can accept a bounded, named efficiency cost to avoid a concentrated harm. Make the trade-off explicit rather than defaulting to fastest.
